A graph begins with a definition

A company can be linked to another through a purchasing relationship, a shared input cost, or competition for the same customers. These connections are economically different. Treating them as one undifferentiated network loses information before a model has even been fitted.

Consider a customer’s demand shock. It may matter for the firms that supply that customer. A disruption at a supplier raises a different question: which customers depend on its output? The same commercial relationship supports two directions of inquiry, with different economic interpretations.

The graph above contains the 475-company research universe and two additional historical counterparties from the filing pilot. Most edges were derived from company profiles intended to describe 2010-era business structure. A small filing pilot adds dated evidence for a handful of links. The explorer keeps those sources separate.

Following a path is the first step

The interactive figure traces supply relationships in either direction, at one or two hops. It identifies companies connected by a possible channel. It does not estimate how much their revenues, profits, or stock prices would change.

Start with Apple to see a profile-based neighborhood. Then select Delta to inspect the smaller set of relationships reviewed against filings. Filtering to reviewed links makes the gap between a plausible network and a documented one visible.

The evidence behind an edge matters as much as the path it creates.

A citation does not settle the relationship

Apple’s 2012–2014 filings describe Intel microprocessors in Macs. That supports a product-component connection. It does not, by itself, establish a direct Apple-to-Intel purchase contract. The explorer therefore labels this edge as a filing candidate rather than a reviewed supplier relationship.

The Delta examples are narrower and better supported. The local pilot reviewed parent-level links to SkyWest and Republic through named regional-carrier subsidiaries in Delta’s 2013–2015 filings. Those links are marked as reviewed, and each disclosure date is available in the source record.

These dates describe when a statement was disclosed. They do not identify when a contract began, and a missing end date does not establish that the relationship continues today.

What remains unresolved

The profiles were reconstructed retrospectively. Their intended 2010 orientation is not proof of an independently archived, point-in-time information set. Some links are flagged as changing during the study; using them as static edges throughout a backtest can misrepresent the information available on a particular date.

The 475-company research universe spans eleven sectors but is still a selected sample. It does not represent all companies or all economic exposures. Shared tags generate many candidate edges; a common business category does not establish a commercial contract. The small filing sample was also used to develop the extraction rules, so its local review does not establish performance on unseen companies or filings.

Most importantly, a path is not an estimate. This explorer assigns no transmission coefficient, causal effect, exposure amount, or expected return to an edge.

Testing the next step

A predictive study needs to separate three questions: whether an edge is supported, whether information moves along it, and whether that information can improve a decision after implementation costs.

The first question calls for frozen extraction rules and review of filings from companies outside the development sample. The second calls for dated graphs and comparisons with sector, correlation, and rewired-network controls on chronological test windows. The third requires portfolio evaluation with explicit turnover and execution assumptions.

The graph is useful because it makes those questions concrete. Its role at this stage is to organize hypotheses and make their sources inspectable.

Sources and implementation

The page uses the project’s existing historical profiles, relationship records, and local filing-review pilot. It makes no new trading-performance claim.
